entities.name: Silahdar Damat Ali Pasha
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Silahdar Damat Ali Pasha (died 1716), an influential Ottoman statesman and military commander, served as Grand Vizier of the Ottoman Empire from April 27, 1713, until his death on August 5, 1716. His tenure marked a critical, albeit brief, period of renewed Ottoman martial ambition following the Treaty of Karlowitz (1699), challenging Habsburg and Venetian dominance in southeastern Europe. Rising through the imperial court as Silahdar (sword-bearer) to Sultan Ahmed III, Ali Pasha epitomized the meritocratic, yet often perilous, career path within the Ottoman military-administrative hierarchy during the early 18th century, a time of both internal reform efforts and external pressures.

As Grand Vizier, Ali Pasha quickly moved to dismantle the peace faction within the Divan and advocated for a more assertive foreign policy. His most significant military undertaking was the Ottoman-Venetian War (1714–1718), specifically leading the campaign to reclaim the Morea (Peloponnese) from Venetian control. In 1715, he personally commanded the Ottoman forces that swiftly recaptured key fortresses like Coron, Modon, and Nauplia, effectively expelling the Venetians from the peninsula in a matter of months. This decisive victory restored a significant territorial loss suffered in the Great Turkish War, boosting Ottoman prestige and demonstrating a surprising resurgence of military capability.

The reconquest of the Morea under Ali Pasha's leadership directly precipitated the Austro-Turkish War of 1716–1718, as Austria, as guarantor of the Treaty of Karlowitz, intervened on Venice's behalf. Ali Pasha led the Ottoman army into Hungary, where he faced Prince Eugene of Savoy's Habsburg forces at the Battle of Petrovaradin on August 5, 1716. Despite numerical superiority, the Ottoman army suffered a catastrophic defeat, and Ali Pasha himself was killed on the battlefield, leading to the collapse of the Ottoman offensive and paving the way for further Habsburg gains.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Silahdar Damat Ali Pasha's leadership briefly revitalized Ottoman military prestige with the reconquest of the Morea, but his subsequent defeat and death at Petrovaradin marked a critical turning point, highlighting the growing military superiority of the Habsburgs and signaling the end of aggressive Ottoman expansionism in Europe.
